extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and narrative writers (filmmakers, novelists) seeking craft guidance on story design and meaning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for discovering, shaping, and dramatizing a story's Controlling Idea (its single-sentence meaning expressed as Value plus Cause) and for constructing the event progressions, Idea-vs-Counter-Idea dynamics, and climax that embody that meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize, don't explain
rubrics_metrics.description: Master storytellers never explain. They dramatize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story's event structure is the means by which you first express, then prove your idea ... without explanation. Dialogue is not a platform for the filmmaker's philosophy; explanatory dialogue or narration seriously diminish a film's quality. A great story authenticates its ideas solely within the dynamics of its events; failure to express a view of life through the pure, honest consequences of human choice and action is a creative defeat no amount of clever language can salvage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Climax must dramatize meaning without explanatory dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's meaning, whether comic or tragic, must be dramatized in an emotionally expressive Story Climax without the aid of explanatory dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Climax should be a final action that excites and moves and feels complete and satisfying. The Controlling Idea should be extractable from this climax; the audience should grasp the idea from the event's consequences rather than from being told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea is a single-sentence meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A true theme (Controlling Idea) is not a word but a sentence—one clear, coherent sentence that expresses a story's irreducible meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Controlling Idea shapes the writer's strategic choices; it is a Creative Discipline guiding what is appropriate or inappropriate in your story, what may be kept and what must be cut. While a story contains many subtleties and subtexts, the cleaner you shape the work around one clear idea, the more meanings audiences will discover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea = Value plus Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Controlling Idea has two components: Value plus Cause. It identifies the positive or negative charge of the story's critical value at the last act's climax, and it identifies the chief reason that this value has changed to its final state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value: the primary value (positive or negative) brought into the protagonist's world by the final action (examples: 'Justice is restored', 'Tyranny prevails', 'Happiness fills our lives'). Cause: the primary reason within the character, society, or environment that brought this value into existence (examples: 'because the protagonist is more violent', 'because it's supported by corrupt forces', 'when we learn to love unconditionally'). A Controlling Idea that states only Value without Cause is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive Controlling Idea from the Story Climax (ask value and cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at your ending and ask: As a result of the climatic action, what value is brought into the protagonist's world? Then trace backward: what is the chief cause by which this value is brought into existence? The sentence composed from answers to these two questions becomes your Controlling Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You do not dictate meaning to the story; you extract idea from action. If a plot works exactly as you planned without surprising you, you may be working too tightly—allow the story to surprise you and let the climax reveal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find idea from action, not impose idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw action from idea, rather idea from action. The story tells you its meaning; you do not dictate meaning to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your inspiration begins with a Premise, character, or image, explore broadly, then mold the film around the idea that the climax reveals. Self-recognition comes when the Story Climax mirrors your inner self; if you don't believe the extracted Controlling Idea, discard it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build progressions by playing Idea against Counter-Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressions build by moving dynamically between the positive and negative charges of the values at stake in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence by sequence (often scene by scene) alternate assertions of the Idea and the Counter-Idea so they argue back and forth, increasing in intensity until they collide at Crisis and produce the Story Climax. Example: crime stories alternate sequences that make the audience feel 'Crime pays' and then 'Crime doesn't pay' until one wins at climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance both sides to avoid slanted argument (avoid didacticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not slant your 'argument.' Compose scenes and sequences that contradict your final statement with as much truth and energy as those that reinforce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your film ends on the Counter-Idea, amplify sequences that make the audience feel the Idea would win, and vice versa. Avoid writing antagonists as fools; create powerful, credible antagonists so a protagonist's victory rings with validity. Designing a story as an undeniable certification of an idea leads to didacticism—a thesis film or sermon that stifles the voice of the other side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow exploration but mold around one idea; avoid packing many ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial exploration, the film must be molded around one idea; the more ideas you try to pack into a story, the more they implode upon themselves until the film says nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore everything during evolution, but ultimately unify the telling around the Controlling Idea. A tight, single-core design increases the richness and multiplicity of meanings audiences will discover rather than collapsing into tangential notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the emotional charge of the Controlling Idea (idealistic/pessimistic/ironic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and their stories can be divided into three categories according to the emotional charge of their Controlling Idea: Idealistic (up-ending), Pessimistic (down-ending), and Ironic (both up and down).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealistic: up-ending expresses optimism and positive values (examples: 'Love fills our lives when...'). Pessimistic: down-ending expresses cynicism or loss (examples: 'Evil triumphs because...'). Ironic: combines positive and negative charges—both are made clear and meaningful (examples: redemption and punitive plots). The chosen charge should guide tone, sequence composition, and climax execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for writing true irony
rubrics_metrics.description: An ironic climax must be a single action that makes both a positive and a negative statement—clearly and honestly motivated—without becoming ambiguous or random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three rules: (1) It must do two things in one action (positive and negative). (2) It must be clear; irony is not ambiguity or coincidence. (3) The double charge must remain separated in the audience's experience so they don't cancel out. Writing irony demands deep wisdom and high craft because it must be honestly motivated and maintain clarity of both charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the Controlling Idea and an artist's responsibility to tell the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Study your Story Climax and extract from it your Controlling Idea. Before proceeding, ask: Is this the truth? Do I believe in the meaning of my story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do not believe it, discard and start again. The author's responsibility is not to cure social ills or uplift society but to tell the truth. Given story's persuasive power, telling an honest truth is an act of social responsibility; do everything possible to get a truthful work into the world, while opposing censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the story to surprise you; combine subject, imagination, and disciplined craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful story design is a combination of the subject found, the imagination at work, and the mind loosely but wisely executing the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a plot works out exactly as first planned, you are not leaving room for imagination and instincts. Your story should surprise you again and again; be open to discoveries as characters and events grow, then shape the design around the discovered Controlling Idea.
